messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Data Scientist
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Affective Expression: Crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Vignette:
Mateo is a 25-year-old data scientist who came to treatment after more than a year of trying to keep one period of his life sealed off in his mind. He is single and lives alone, and when he first described the event that still follows him, he did so in fragments, stopping and starting, as if the pieces would not stay in order long enough to tell straight through. His younger child cousin, whom he helped care for during a medical crisis, became suddenly and frighteningly ill. Mateo was one of the adults present during the emergency, and what remains with him is not a smooth story but a set of searing moments: the child struggling for life, adults crying, the smell of sweat in a crowded room and later in the ambulance and hospital, and the sound of sirens cutting through everything. Even now he says that when he tries to recount what happened, he cannot place what came first and what came after. The memory feels so extreme to him that part of him still reacts as if it could not have really happened in his own life. Yet when it comes back, it does not feel distant or doubtful in his body; it brings back the same terror he felt at the time.

In the weeks after the illness, Mateo tried to function by forcing the whole experience out of awareness. He worked hard not to think about it, cutting off images as soon as they appeared and shifting his attention back to coding problems, dashboards, or whatever task was in front of him. He had also come to believe he could not allow himself anger of any kind. He described clamping down on it immediately, never letting himself feel or express it, even in ordinary situations. If a colleague interrupted him in a meeting or a stranger behaved rudely on the train, he would go quiet and rigid rather than acknowledge irritation. He spoke about this as a rule he had for himself, as though any strong feeling might break something open that he was barely containing already.

Certain reminders entered his life with painful force. Sirens are the clearest. Working as a data scientist in a downtown office, he cannot control the sounds outside: ambulances passing during the day, emergency vehicles cutting through traffic below the windows, a sudden burst of noise on his walk from the train. When he hears one, his body reacts before he can think. He startles sharply, his chest tightens, and he feels a rush through his whole body that makes it hard to stay present with what he is doing. At times he has had to step away from his desk and wait for the reaction to settle. Crying is another potent trigger. If someone tears up during a conversation, or if he hears crying in a film or in public, he is immediately brought close to the emotional atmosphere of that day. The smell of sweat or body odour also affects him in a way that embarrasses him; in crowded elevators, on public transit after work, or in the gym locker room he can suddenly feel pulled back toward the emergency, his body responding as if danger is near.

He has gradually organized his life around staying away from medical settings. He will take a longer route to avoid passing the hospital near his apartment. He looks away or crosses the street when he sees an ambulance parked outside a building. He postpones routine physical examinations because even the thought of a clinic feels unbearable. These decisions have accumulated quietly. Friends and relatives have noticed that he makes excuses when someone suggests visiting an ill family member or meeting near the medical center. He knows this has narrowed his world, but in the moment avoiding feels like the only way to keep himself steady.

At night Mateo has particular difficulty settling into sleep. He lies in bed feeling that he needs to remain alert, as if letting go of vigilance would be unsafe. Ordinary noises in his building can make him jump. A door closing in the hallway, a car horn outside, something dropped by an upstairs neighbor—sounds that others would dismiss can jolt him fully awake. He often starts the next workday tired, already strained before opening his laptop. He is frustrated by how much energy goes into monitoring his surroundings and trying not to let his mind drift toward the illness and emergency.

What finally brought him to seek help was a recent incident at work: an ambulance siren passed during a team meeting just as a coworker became tearful over a personal matter. Mateo felt an immediate, intense bodily surge and had to leave the room abruptly. He was shaken not only by the reaction itself but by how unreal and disorganized the memory still felt afterward, as though he could neither fully remember it nor fully escape it. Coming to therapy, he says he wants to be able to hear a siren or walk past a clinic without feeling overtaken. What frightens him most is the sense that the terror is still waiting just under the surface, ready to return in full whenever something in the world resembles that day.
